notes:
I've written notes for every verse, but they're uneven. My tool limit ran out before I could reach Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu) or bibleodyssey.org sources, so those views aren't covered. Notes on vv. 22–26 are thin. The NET Bible notes below are only the ones quoted on Precept Austin. The verse where traditions really split is vv. 19–21; the main differences are collected after the verse notes.

---

**v. 1**
- Peter and John were very different men, now working together. Spurgeon thinks John brought Peter back after his denial. The two went up daily, not just on the Sabbath, which suggests prayer was their way of life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- The NET note (quoted there) says the first Jewish Christians were still taking part in Judaism's institutions. The prayer times were 9 AM, 3 PM and sunset. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- Morgan says they went for the prayer that followed the afternoon sacrifice, not for the sacrifice itself, because Jesus' sacrifice had fulfilled that system. Calvin (Reformed) thinks they went mainly to find a chance to spread the gospel. Hughes notes the ninth hour was when Jesus cried "It is finished." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Spurgeon sees the old order gradually "melting" into the new here. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 2**
- The man wanted to be supported in his condition; God had something better in mind; Jesus wanted to completely change his condition. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Judaism had a strong tradition of alms-giving, so the Beautiful Gate was a sensible place for him to beg. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Matthew Henry says he was lame from birth, not by accident, probably from a condition that weakened his limbs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/acts-3.html

**v. 3**
- Henry: alms were the most he expected. Henry also asks why he didn't ask for more, if he knew these were Christ's messengers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_003.cfm

**v. 4–5**
- People usually avoid looking at beggars. When the apostles looked straight at him, he probably expected a big gift. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Guzik calls this expectation "faith, plain and simple," even though the man expected less than God meant to give. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- A different emphasis: The man was not expecting a healing; he was only expecting a handout. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 6**
- Peter had no money, but he did have authority from Jesus to heal the sick. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Calvin: Peter means he would gladly have given money if he had it. Whatever God gives us is meant to be used in love for others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-6.html
- Henry: It is not often that Christ's friends and favourites have abundance of the wealth of this world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-6.html
- Gill: they may have had only the church's common fund, and no money could be carried into the temple anyway. Barnes: "what I have" doesn't mean the power was Peter's own; it came from Christ. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/acts/3-6.html
- On "Nazarene": Peter used a despised name, showing that God uses the lowly, and that the man from Nazareth is alive and healing from heaven. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- **Wealth and the church:** Guzik tells a story, "perhaps true," of a cardinal saying the church no longer had to say "silver and gold I do not have." A monk replied that neither could it say "rise up and walk." Guzik also quotes LaSor: the church exists to release God's redemptive work, not just to make people's present condition more bearable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Older sermons (Biblical Illustrator) also contrast the apostles' poverty and power with papal wealth. https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/3-6.htm
- Guzik's summary applies this to modern teaching: real blessing comes from turning away from sin, not simply through material comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- I found no source naming prosperity or word-of-faith teaching directly.

**v. 7**
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel, charismatic-leaning) says Peter received the "gift of faith" of 1 Corinthians 12:9 at this moment. He acted on the Holy Spirit's specific prompting, not on a whim. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- We have no reason to believe that Peter made a habit taking every lame man he saw, pulling them up by the hand. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/walking-leaping-praising/
- Morgan says "feet," "ankle-bones" and "leaping up" are technical medical words, fitting for Luke the physician. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- The healing was instant; the man needed no therapy to walk, though he had never walked before. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 8**
- The healed man did three things: he stayed with the apostles, used his new strength, and praised God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Henry sees Isaiah 35:6 fulfilled: Then shall the lame man leap as a hart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/acts-3.html
- He praised God, not his "positive mental attitude" or his own faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- GotQuestions compares his gratitude with the one grateful leper of Luke 17. https://www.gotquestions.org/walking-and-leaping-and-praising-God.html

**v. 9–10**
- He was over 40 (Acts 4:22) and a familiar sight, so Jesus must have passed him many times. Guzik's explanation: God's timing is just as important as His will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Deffinbaugh (bible.org) sees the healing as a sign of blessing and a foreshadowing of the messianic blessings of the kingdom. https://bible.org/seriespage/6-lame-excuse-preaching-gospel-acts-31-26

**v. 11**
- He wasn't holding on for support; perhaps from gratitude, or fear and surprise. https://enduringword.com/better-than-a-testimony/
- Wonder alone saves no one: it merely aroused interest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/

**v. 12**
- Peter didn't hold a testimony or healing service. He preached the gospel, knowing faith comes by hearing God's word (Romans 10:17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Guzik warns that some preachers today imply healing comes from their own spirituality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- John Phillips takes the verse as a blow against trusting "saints" and against the idea that holy men build up merit to work miracles for others. Steven Cole: we are only clay vessels. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 13**
- Naming the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob made it clear Peter meant Israel's own God. "Servant" points to Isaiah 42 and 52–53. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- An early Targum treats Isaiah 42:1 as being about the Messiah. Peter calls Jesus God's Servant (*pais*) to Jewish audiences to show he is the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- Guilt for Jesus' death: Guzik says Jews and Romans shared it, and ultimately "our sin" put Jesus on the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/

**v. 14–15**
- "Holy One" is used over 40 times in the Old Testament as a title for God, so Guzik reads it as calling Jesus divine. Peter says "you" far more often here than at Pentecost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- The irony: they chose a murderer, Barabbas, over Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Spurgeon: "Every sin in the essence of it is a killing of God." Thompson: Christ's blood can condemn or cleanse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 16 (whose faith?)**
- Precept Austin: Peter seems to mean his own faith, not to the man's faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- The Moody Bible Commentary agrees the healing didn't come from the man's faith. Miracles in Acts mainly prove that Jesus is alive and is the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- The NET note (quoted there) says it's unclear he believed beforehand, and calls this possibly a "grace-faith miracle." https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- Pentecostal view: Stanley Horton (Logion Press, an Assemblies of God publisher) reads it as the man's faith. He allows that it may mean the apostles' faith, with the healing then leading the man to believe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- Guzik: the "name" means Jesus' authority, and even the faith came through Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- POSB (quoted on Precept Austin) takes this further, in a Reformed-style direction: faith is a gift started by the Spirit, because a dead spirit can't move toward God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 17**
- Peter still calls them "brethren," though twice he has said they denied Jesus, something he had done himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/

**v. 18**
- Neither Jewish nor Roman authorities could block God's plan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/
- Precept Austin: God used their ignorance just as He had foretold. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 19**
- Barclay: ancient ink sat on top of papyrus and could be wiped off with a sponge; God wipes out sin the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-19.html
- Grammar: the Pulpit Commentary says the Greek can't mean "when" (KJV) but "that so there may come." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-19.htm
- What are the "times of refreshing"? Readings vary:
  - Clarke (Methodist): the whole reign of grace now, peace and joy for believers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-19.html
  - Gill (Baptist): relief for believers when judgment fell on the nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-19.html
  - Barnes: the gospel age, lasting to the end of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-19.htm
  - Spurgeon: possibly revivals in the church; in context, the second coming. https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/3-19.htm
  - Ellicott: Israel, as a nation, did not repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-19.htm

**v. 20–21 (the main dividing point)**
- **Dispensational view:** Constable and Ryrie (bible.org): the "times of refreshing" and "restoration" mean the millennial kingdom. Israel's repentance would bring forgiveness for individuals, and for the nation, the Messiah's return to reign. https://bible.org/question/if-jews-had-accepted-christ-their-messiah-would-earthly-kingdom-have-been-established-then
- Constable also quotes a view that this was *not* a re-offer of the kingdom, since Jesus wasn't personally present. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-19.html
- MacArthur (gty, Baptist) calls it just the same standing offer of the kingdom. He links "restoration" to Acts 1:6. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1713/the-necessity-of-repentance
- Guzik: Israel's national acceptance of Jesus must come before His return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/Acts+3/
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees the kingdom's days were delayed by the unbelief of Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-19.htm
- **Non-dispensational readings:** Coffman (Restoration Movement): the second coming comes at the *end* of the restoration, not its beginning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-20.html
- JFB: the period between ascension and return, setting right all the disorders of the fall. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-21.htm
- Ellicott: restoration began with Christ's death. He ties it to Matthew 17:11 and Malachi as a moral and spiritual restoration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-21.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): restoration happens in each converted soul and will be complete when the work becomes universal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/3-21.html
- **"Heaven must receive":** Ellicott: "must receive and keep." Matthew Poole: heaven holds Christ's true body as a real place holds a body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/3-21.htm
- I found no Lutheran source on this verse to compare with Poole.
- **Universalism:** supporters of *apokatastasis* (universal reconciliation) cite this verse, the word's only use in Scripture. GotQuestions asks whether that is biblical. https://www.gotquestions.org/apocatastasis.html

**v. 22–23**
- The prophet promised in Deuteronomy 18:18 is fulfilled in Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_commentaries
- Jesus was both *the* Prophet and the one all the prophets spoke about. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary

**v. 24**
- The crowd was seeing what all the prophets foretold. https://www.gotquestions.org/walking-and-leaping-and-praising-God.html

**v. 25**
- "Families" here means kindreds or peoples in the broad sense. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_314-15

**v. 26**
- "Servant" (*pais*) again marks Jesus as the Messiah for Jewish hearers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-3-commentary
- God's blessing is turning people from their sins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-3/

---

**Main differences between traditions**
1. **vv. 19–21:** a literal kingdom offered to Israel (Constable, Ryrie, MacArthur, Pulpit), against present gospel-age or spiritual readings (Clarke, Barnes, Gill, JFB, Coffman, Ellicott).
2. **v. 16:** whose faith healed him. Pentecostal Horton says the man's; Precept Austin, Moody and the NET note lean to the apostles' faith or to grace alone.
3. **v. 21:** universalist use of "restoration of all things."
